Controls (quoted speech, hypotheticals, unrelated negations, changes over time, other people's actions, separate occasions, uncertainty) and self-corrections are labelled not contradictory. A contradictory answer is labelled at most Good.

cases.answer: One strength I would bring is staying calm and organised when a shift goes wrong. Last winter on a busy medical ward, two of my six patients deteriorated in the same hour while the evening medicines were due. I was the nurse responsible for that bay, so keeping all six safe was my job. I asked the healthcare assistant to take over the routine observations, and I called the doctor about the sicker patient. Every patient had their evening medicines on time and both were stable by 9 pm. I learned that asking for help early is part of being organised.

cases.answer: On a night shift on the surgical ward, I had to tell a man's daughter that his operation had been cancelled for the second time after he had fasted all day. Before I spoke to her, I asked the surgeon for the new date so I could give her a real answer. I took her to the quiet room, told her plainly what had happened and said I was sorry for the wait. I gave her the new date and the ward phone number. She was upset but thanked me, and he had his operation 2 days later. I learned to get the facts before the conversation, not during it.

cases.answer: When I cannot do both well, I do the patient assessment first and shorten the medication round, which means some doses run up to 30 minutes late. I choose that because a missed change in a patient's condition can do more harm than a slightly late routine dose. I tell the nurse in charge and the doctor which doses will be late, and I tell the patients when I will be back. For example, last month I found a man with new chest pain during my assessments, so I called the doctor and gave the remaining medicines half an hour late. He was seen within ten minutes.

With a patient who disagrees with how often I check his observations, I would sit down, ask what bothers him and listen without interrupting. I would explain in plain words why the checks matter after his surgery and offer to group them with his pain review so he is woken less. That means fewer separate checks, which I would accept as long as his early warning score stays reliable. I would write the agreement in his care plan, tell the next shift, and check with him the next morning that it is working.
